plan.contextChunk: This figure has two panels, (a) and (b), each drawing a convex polygon over labeled points in the plane. In (a) a light gray polygon labeled Q_j fills the right portion; its boundary runs from p_0 at the bottom left up to p_j at the top, right through p_k and two unlabeled black dots, down the right side to p_2, and back along the bottom through p_1 to p_0. A darker gray triangle is attached along the left, with corners p_0, p_j, and a further point p_i lying outside to the left, so that the two shaded regions together form a larger polygon whose boundary now passes through p_i. In (b) the hull boundary is a thick gray chain from p_0 rightward to p_1, up the right side, and back across the top through p_j; at the left a thin-outlined light gray triangle has corners p_i, p_r just to its right, and p_0 at the bottom, and a point p_t sits inside that triangle. Dashed segments join p_i and p_r to p_t, and a small arc marks the angle at p_t. Placing the panels side by side contrasts a point that enlarges the hull with a point enclosed by three others and therefore incapable of being a hull vertex. The pair underpins the correctness argument for Graham's scan, where each newly considered point either joins the stack or forces an earlier point off it.

interactions.label: Turn case
interactions.teaches: Turn direction at the stack top decides hull membership: a left turn means the new point extends the hull, a nonleft turn means the tested point is interior and cannot be a hull vertex

interactions.label: Step Graham scan
interactions.teaches: Each Graham-scan iteration tests one angle at the stack top: on a left turn the candidate point is pushed and the shaded hull grows, on a nonleft turn the top point is removed because it lies inside the triangle formed by its neighbors

interactions.label: Inspect a point
interactions.teaches: Selecting p_i, p_j, p_r, or p_t highlights the supporting hull edge or enclosing triangle, showing exactly which surrounding points prove the selected point lies on or inside the hull

demo_steps.title: Left turn expands the hull
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a), the angle at p_j is a left turn, so p_i is pushed: the darker triangle p_0 p_j p_i is added to Q_j and the hull boundary now passes through p_i.

demo_steps.title: Nonleft turn exposes an interior point
demo_steps.narration: In panel (b), the turn at p_r is nonleft: p_r lies inside triangle p_i p_t ... p_0 with p_t interior, so p_r is popped from the stack and can never be a hull vertex.

demo_steps.title: Inspect the witnesses
demo_steps.narration: Click p_t or p_r to highlight the dashed triangle and angle arc — the enclosing triangle is the witness proving a nonleft-turn point is interior, the core of Graham's scan correctness.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A point that makes a nonleft turn at the stack top lies inside the triangle formed by neighboring points, so popping it is always safe — only left-turn points can be convex-hull vertices.

Label Q_j centered in the light region. All vertex markers small black dots; labels in italic serif. Highlighting on click should tint the relevant triangle or hull edge, and the toggle cross-fades between the two panel states rather than showing both at once.

authoredContext: Theorem 33.1 (Correctness of Graham’s scan) If GRAHAM-SCAN executes on a set Q of points, where jQj _x0015_ 3, then at termination, the stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Q/ in counterclockwise order. Proof After line 2, we have the sequence of points hp1; p2; : : : ; pmi. Let us define, for i D 2; 3; : : : ; m, the subset of points Qi D fp0; p1; : : : ; pi g. The points in Q Qm are those that were removed because they had the same polar angle relative to p0 as some point in Qm; these points are not in CH.Q/, and so CH.Qm/ D CH.Q/. Thus, it suffices to show that when GRAHAM-SCAN terminates, the stack S consists of the vertices of CH.Qm/ in counterclockwise order, when listed from bottom to top. Note that just as p0, p1, and pm are vertices of CH.Q/, the points p0, p1, and pi are all vertices of CH.Qi/. The proof uses the following loop invariant: At the start of each iteration of the for loop of lines 9–12, stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Qi1/ in counterclockwise order
